research_question: Can a retrievable bacterial-cellulose/SCOBY marine sorbent compete economically with current polypropylene oil-only pads/booms when judged by recovered oil rather than headline absorption capacity?

core_formulae.total_cost_per_kg_recovered_oil: BC_material_cost + drying + hydrophobic_treatment + sleeve + labor + energy + retrieval + waste_handling, all normalized by measured recovered oil

frozen_model_assumptions.note: 0.60 is the current internal M1 press-recovery gate, not a measured SCOBY result. Oil density is a scenario assumption used only to normalize commercial litre/gallon capacity to approximate kg.

commercial_reference_points.product: New Pig PIG Oil-Only Absorbent Mat Pad MAT403
commercial_reference_points.comparison_rule: Nominal absorption-capacity benchmark only; not a measured recovered-oil cost.

commercial_reference_points.product: New Pig oil-only absorbent boom via VWR, 3 in x 10 ft
commercial_reference_points.comparison_rule: Nominal boom capacity benchmark only; BC model is deliberately stricter because it includes a 60% recovered-oil fraction.

BC_cost_scenarios_from_literature.source_note: 2026 simplified techno-economic analysis of BC as a bioplastic reported MPSP about 1.89 USD/kg under its modeled assumptions.
A 2025 review cites a large-scale SuperPro model in which beet molasses reduced BC production cost to about 14.8 USD/kg.
A 2025 co-culture review cites a techno-economic assessment around 63.8 USD/kg dry BC.

break_even_against_MAT403_2_33_USD_per_n.interpretation: At approximately 14.8 USD/kg dry BC, the existing technical M1 threshold of 10 g/g is only borderline economic before drying, sleeve, labor and treatment. A practical low-cost target should therefore be closer to >=20 g/g unless BC is obtained as a very low-cost byproduct.

one_meter_boom_reference_capacity_match.interpretation: At the central 14.8 USD/kg scenario, q around 20-40 g/g leaves roughly 6.8-8.1 USD/m of the reference boom price for sleeve, drying/treatment and manufacturing while targeting about 2.11 kg recovered oil per meter. At 63.8 USD/kg BC, q must be much higher to leave room for non-BC costs.

production_yield_context.source_note: A 2025 study using vinegar residue medium reported 5.36 g/L BC, compared with 1.13 g/L on Hestrin-Schramm control.
production_yield_context.boundary: This is not a kombucha-factory production forecast. Yield depends strongly on strain, medium, reactor, time and purification.

GROW_TO_SORB.description: Grow BC specifically for oil-spill sorbents.
GROW_TO_SORB.reason: Fermentation infrastructure, labor, purification and pore-preserving drying can dominate cost; published BC production-cost estimates span more than an order of magnitude.

WASTE_TO_BOOM.description: Collect kombucha/KBC pellicle that is already a low-value coproduct or residue, then wash, structurally process, contain in a retrievable sleeve and use once.
WASTE_TO_BOOM.reason: A 2025 KBC review explicitly describes kombucha pellicle as a coproduct often lacking economic value, which can remove much of the fermentation-feedstock burden if collection and quality control are workable.

economic_promotion_gates.E0_TECHNICAL: Keep M1_G1 >=10 g/g as a technical viability floor, not an economic win criterion.
economic_promotion_gates.E1_LOW_COST_TARGET: Prefer >=20 g/g surrogate-oil uptake with >=60% contained press recovery in marine conditions, unless measured dry-BC delivered cost is below approximately 10-15 USD/kg.
economic_promotion_gates.E2_STRONG_TARGET: >=40 g/g with >=60% recovery is economically attractive even under substantially higher BC-cost scenarios, before non-BC costs.
economic_promotion_gates.E3_PER_METER: Pilot 1 m cartridge should target <=9.44 USD/m total manufacturing cost while recovering about 2.1 kg oil-equivalent per meter under the frozen test protocol, or demonstrate a superior cost-per-recovered-kg metric.
economic_promotion_gates.E4_REAL_METRIC: Promotion requires measured TOTAL_COST_PER_KG_RECOVERED_OIL below the selected commercial reference after including drying, treatment, sleeve, labor, energy, retrieval and spent-sorbent handling.
economic_promotion_gates.E5_REPLICATE: Economic PASS requires at least two independent BC batches and one commercial control tested under the same liquid, drain and recovery protocol.

janus_tranception.forward: BC_SOURCE_COST -> PROCESSING_COST -> q_OIL -> MARINE_RETENTION -> RETRIEVAL -> PRESS_RECOVERY -> RECOVERED_OIL_KG -> COST_PER_RECOVERED_KG -> COMMERCIAL_COMPARISON
janus_tranception.promotion_rule: No ECONOMIC_PASS until the same measured M1/M2 batch supplies q, recovery, retrieval, process cost and commercial-control comparison.

preliminary_verdict.plain_language: The concept can plausibly be cheaper than polypropylene sorbents if SCOBY/KBC is sourced as a low-cost byproduct and marine q_oil lands around 20-40 g/g or better with >=60% recoverable oil. It is unlikely to be cheap if BC is grown as an expensive specialty material and only reaches ~10 g/g.
highest_value_next_measurements: actual dry BC cost per kg for each D0-D3 route
actual sleeve plus manufacturing cost per meter
